implementation_notes: On the JVM the provider supplies the endpoint: a JMSConsumer with setMessageListener(...), or an MDB whose onMessage is invoked by the container, receives jakarta.jms.Message objects while the provider owns the session, redelivery and transaction boundaries. The endpoint then only translates payloads into domain calls and decides ack behaviour within the provider's contract; write the session loop by hand only when no listener container is available.
pitfalls: onMessage runs on a provider thread and one session delivers serially: blocking inside the listener stalls that whole session, so use one session per worker.
With container-managed transactions a thrown exception rolls the message back, so catch-and-swallow silently turns into endless redelivery; decide the exception contract explicitly.
Message bodies are provider-specific when using ObjectMessage; prefer a portable payload (TextMessage/bytes) and an explicit mapper.

variants.name: KafkaConsumer poll loop with offset commits
variants.implementation_notes: Kafka has no listener container: the endpoint is the application-owned poll loop. consumer.subscribe(topics) followed by while(running) { poll(Duration) ... commitSync() } with manual offsets is at-least-once, and the offsets are the acknowledgement. Choose this when the log semantics are wanted or no framework owns the listener; the JMS listener container fits better when the broker provides queue-style redelivery and the framework should own transactions.
pitfalls: poll() is the liveness signal: if handling exceeds max.poll.interval.ms the consumer leaves the group and its partitions are rebalanced, so bound per-poll work or hand records to worker threads with pause()/offset discipline.
KafkaConsumer is not thread-safe; commit offsets after processing (not after poll) or a crash between the two silently skips records.
Committing offsets before handling completes converts at-least-once into at-most-once.
